# Repair and self-healing — function ontology

**Card 10 · source workbook `ontology/xlsx/Nature_Repair_Ontology_v2.xlsx` · generated by `scripts/build-knowledge.js` — do not edit by hand.**

## Scope boundary

Covers how living systems prevent, detect, stabilise, seal and rebuild damage, and how those sequences transfer to engineered materials and systems. Sixteen strategies (NR01–NR16) with the S1–S10 sub-strategy vocabulary bridging to the main ontology. Does not cover adhesion for its own sake (card 14), thermal damage prevention (card 12), or pattern formation (cards 11a–11d). Complete: 60 mapped papers.

## Strategies

| ID | Strategy | Biological model | Engineering-neutral rule | Use when | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NR01 | Protect / prevent damage | Tree bark; arthropod exoskeleton; skin; functional plant surfaces | Put a robust, task-specific layer ahead of vulnerable functions; design that layer to be renewable or sacrificial when possible. | High exposure frequency; surface-dominated failure; contamination/corrosion/fouling risk | Added thickness/mass can impede transport or flexibility |
| NR02 | Contain / compartmentalize | Trees — compartmentalization of decay (CODIT); immune barriers | If full repair is expensive or risky, isolate the failing zone and preserve the rest of the system. | Distributed systems; non-critical local loss acceptable; propagation risk high | Local capacity is sacrificed |
| NR03 | Rapid plug / seal | Blood clotting; invertebrate hemolymph clotting; plant wound secretio… | Prioritize a fast sealing mechanism that stabilizes the defect even if it does not yet restore load-bearing performance. | Leakage, ingress, corrosion exposure, puncture-like damage | Fast closure can obstruct later reconstruction or provide little mechanical str… |
| NR04 | Adhesive rejoin | Mussel byssus / adhesive plaque; tissue interfaces | Design the damaged interface itself as an active repair zone using reversible, water-compatible, high-affinity interactions. | Delamination, wet adhesion, coatings, tissue interfaces | High bond density can reduce chain mobility |
| NR05 | Reservoir release | Weeping fig latex cells; secretory cells; biological vesicle-like sto… | Separate reactive chemistry from the host until a damage-specific trigger releases it. | Sparse unpredictable cracks; manufacturing can tolerate inclusions | Finite payload; capsules change host mechanics |
| NR06 | Vascular transport / replenishment | Blood vessels; plant vasculature; refillable biological transport | Use a connected distribution network when damage is recurrent, internal, or requires more material than a local reservoir can hold. | Repeated same-zone damage; large components; inaccessible internal cracks | Network volume and complexity; network itself can fail |
| NR07 | Layer / renew / shed | Snake molting; tree bark; lotus wax; plant abscission | When the outer layer is expendable, replace it instead of repeatedly repairing the same degraded material. | High-cycle surface wear; coatings; self-cleaning; replaceable skins | Consumes material and creates waste |
| NR08 | Dynamic rebond | Protein networks; extracellular-matrix-like hydrogels; mussel-inspire… | Build reversible bonds into the material so the same chemistry can repeatedly disconnect and reconnect. | Small gaps; repeat damage; soft/semirigid polymers; hydrogels | Strength–mobility trade-off |
| NR09 | Sacrificial dissipation + recovery | Mussel byssus; bone; nacre; tough biological tissues | Give the structure reversible 'fuses' that fail before the main load path and can reset afterward. | Impact, fatigue, stretchable structures | Hysteresis / residual strain / slower recovery |
| NR10 | Hierarchical crack control | Tooth enamel; nacre; bone; fibrous biological composites | Separate load bearing and healing across scales so strong domains do not eliminate the mobility needed for repair. | Load-bearing composites where conventional self-healing is too soft | More reinforcement can suppress healing mobility |
| NR11 | Biomineralize / regrow missing material | Bone/shell formation; bacteria, fungi, algae | Use the damaged void as a reactor: bring precursors to it and grow a compatible solid phase in situ. | Porous mineral materials; wet environments; inaccessible microcracks if agents are embedd… | Strong dependence on environmental window and access |
| NR12 | Living remodeling / regeneration | Skin; bone; tendon; nerve-supporting regenerative tissue | Treat repair as ongoing remodeling with removal and replacement, not a one-time crack closure event. | Biohybrid/living materials; regenerative interfaces; long-service adaptive systems | Slow and resource-intensive |
| NR13 | Dissolve → redistribute → redeploy | Fibrinolysis in blood vessels (engineering analogue in Li–S electroly… | When failure is caused by material becoming trapped in the wrong phase/location, remobilize and recycle it instead of adding new material. | Batteries, deposition/fouling systems, crystallization-driven failure | Mobility can create unwanted shuttle/leakage |
| NR14 | Adaptive reconfiguration | Muscle; chameleon nanocrystal spacing; bound-water networks; sea-cucu… | Design kinetics so the material is compliant when useful and temporarily stiff/locked when disturbance rate exceeds a threshold. | Impact protection; adaptive stiffness; variable environment | Narrow operating window / kinetic mismatch |

| NR16 | Staged / temporal repair | Hemostasis → inflammation/proliferation → remodeling; plant multistag… | Allocate different repair jobs to different timescales and coordinate handoff between them. | Complex damage; corrosion protection; structural repair where speed and completeness conf… | Coordination complexity |

## Challenge triggers

Classify the damage first, then select. These are the lines that decide when this ontology is the right one to reach for.

| Challenge | Qualifiers | Prioritise | Combine with | Reasoning rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Urgent fluid leak / ingress through a new crack | Need seconds–hours response; strength can recover later | NR03 | NR05/NR06 + NR16 | Stabilize homeostasis first: stop flow before optimizing structural restoration. |
| Crack repeatedly reopens at same location | Recurrence high; local payload may exhaust | NR06 or NR08 | NR15 + NR16 | Favor replenishable transport or intrinsic reversible networks over one-shot reservoirs. |
| Deep internal crack with no maintenance access | Repair location uncertain; resources must reach depth | NR06 + NR11 | NR15 | Make access/transport a hard feasibility filter before chemistry selection. |
| Large gap; faces cannot physically re-contact | Damage volume large | NR06/NR11/NR12 | NR03 | If re-contact is impossible, supply or grow new material rather than rely only on rebonding. |
| Very small recurrent microdamage in polymer | Faces can re-contact; many cycles desired | NR08 | NR09/NR15 | Use reversible molecular networks when damage is small and repeated. |
| High-load structural material must remain stiff | Healing–strength trade-off is severe | NR10 + NR09 | NR08 | Spatially separate load bearing from healing and use sacrificial interfaces. |
| Impact / high strain-rate hazard | Need temporary stiffening + dissipation | NR14 + NR09 | NR10 | Match bond kinetics to loading rate so interactions 'lock' under fast loading but recover later. |
| Corrosive environment after surface cracking | Prevent ingress and restore barrier fast | NR01 + NR03 | NR16 + NR15 | Treat barrier restoration as its own function; follow with deeper repair where needed. |
| Concrete microcracks in moist/alkaline environment | Water available; crack width and agent viability matter | NR11 | NR05/NR06/NR16 | Use biomineralization when ecology and resource access match the substrate. |
| Concrete crack exposed at surface but not deep | External treatment possible | NR11 + external intervention mode | NR03 | Use surface-applied biorepair but quantify penetration separately. |
| Opaque internal concrete; proposed algae repair | No light inside bulk | Alternative NR11 agent (bacteria/… | NR06 | Reject biological models whose required environmental resource cannot reach the defect. |
| Surface wears/fouls continuously | Damage is distributed and routine | NR07 + NR01 | NR15 | Renew the surface continuously or periodically instead of detecting and patching every microdefect. |
| Local damage threatens to spread but local function is expendable | Propagation risk > local loss | NR02 | NR07/NR16 | Contain and sacrifice the local zone if that preserves system survival. |
| Device crack causes signal drift | Mechanical + electrical functions both matter | NR15 + NR08 | NR10 | Require recovery of the actual device signal pathway, not only visible crack closure. |
| Deposition/precipitate becomes trapped in wrong location or phase | Matter is present but unavailable | NR13 | NR06/NR15 | Remobilize the stranded matter and return it to the working cycle. |
| Multiple conflicting repair timescales | Need immediate stabilization + long-term restoration | NR16 | NR03/NR06/NR08/NR11/NR15 | Assign functions to time: stabilize → mobilize → reconstruct → remodel/verify. |
| Unknown failure location in a large asset | Distributed damage; monitoring costly | NR15 + NR06 | NR05 | Distribute both sensing and repair access; avoid assuming a known damage coordinate. |
| Resource-constrained autonomous system | No high heat/external service; long mission | NR08/NR14 if ambient-compatible | NR06 if refillable onboard | Treat energy/resource budget as a selection constraint equal to healing efficiency. |

## Maturity guide

- **The five levels**
- **Lab-scale** — Demonstrated in a paper, single samples, controlled conditions. Unknown whether it survives manufacture.
- **Pilot / scaled demo** — Larger batches or a pilot line. Not commercial.
- **In production** — Someone manufactures with it today. Always name WHICH industry — mature in food packaging can be lab-scale in medical devices.
- **Commodity** — Several suppliers, standard equipment, known price.
- **N/A — biological mechanism** — The row anchors a natural mechanism, not an engineered system. Maturity does not apply.
- **Two mandatory companions**
- **Maturity evidence** — What the level rests on: a single paper, several groups, a patent, a reported pilot line, or a product on sale. 'One 2023 paper' and 'three companies manufacturing' are different confidence levels en…
- **Scale-up blocker** — The specific barrier: yield, rate, uniformity, equipment cost, feedstock availability, or regulatory approval. One sentence. This is what turns maturity from information into action.
- **Read this before trusting the column**
- **Most values are INFERRED, not verified** — Rows marked 'Lab-scale (assumed)' were inferred from the type of paper, not confirmed by research. They are shaded red and marked [VERIFY]. Do not let the engine present an inferred level as a checke…
- **Guessing here is expensive** — A founder plans timelines and fundraising on maturity. An unverified guess presented confidently is the failure mode most likely to lose a technical founder's trust. 'Searched, did not resolve' is a…
- **Discussion volume is not maturity** — A widely discussed technique sounds closer to production than it is.
